title: Adams' Synchronological Chart of Universal History
summary: Sebastian C. Adams's 23-foot wall chart of the world's history from Creation to the 1870s: the Bible's family lines along the top, the nations as streams of color below, and hundreds of small pictures of the people, buildings and inventions of every age.
credit: Scan of the third edition (1878): [David Rumsey Map Collection, David Rumsey Map Center, Stanford Libraries](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~226099~5505934), no. 6000.013, shared under [CC BY-NC-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/3.0/) by way of the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/adams-synchronological-chart-of-universal-history); this copy is shared on the same terms. The marks and links on the chart are the collection's own.
about:
## About the chart

Sebastian C. Adams, a teacher and Presbyterian minister in Oregon, first published this chart in 1871 as a *Chronological Chart of Ancient, Modern and Biblical History*. It sets 6,000 years of history side by side on one long sheet, about 23 feet wide, so that a reader can see at a glance what was happening everywhere in the world at the same time. That is what *synchronological* means.

The stream of time runs from left to right. Upright pillars mark each hundred years and thinner red lines the decades. The Bible's family lines, from Adam through Noah, Abraham and David to Jesus, run along the top. Below them each nation flows as a band of color, widening as it grows, splitting when it divides and ending when it is conquered. Small pictures stand beside the streams: the pyramids, the Tower of Babel, the kings and prophets, the printing press, the steam engine.

## Reading its dates

Adams based every date on the system of Archbishop James Ussher, who in the 1650s counted back through the Bible's genealogies and reached 4004 BC for Creation and 2348 BC for the Flood. Adams explains that he kept Ussher's system because most of the dates in the history books of his day were built on it, while saying plainly that "Moses assigns no date to this Creation."

Read the chart as a picture of how a 19th-century Christian historian saw the whole of history, not as the last word on its dates. Many Christians still hold a young earth and a chronology close to Ussher's. Others, together with most historians and archaeologists today, place Egypt's early kings, the first cities and the earth itself much earlier, and read the genealogies of Genesis as not meant to be added up into a calendar. The topic [Dating the Kings](/topic/regnal-chronology) shows how the dates of Israel's and Judah's kings are worked out today.

## Using this page

Drag the chart to move along it; scroll, pinch or use the buttons to zoom in until the smallest writing is clear. Each colored mark is something the collection has linked: open it to read about it, go to the passage in the books here, or read more on Wikipedia. The list below the chart has the same marks in the chart's order, and *Go to* takes you to any year.

From the Exodus to Solomon's Temple
The kings, to the fall of Jerusalem
The Greek kingdoms and the coming of Rome
Jesus, the apostles and the Roman Empire

entries.p: Cain, Adam's firstborn, heads the upper line of his descendants. The chart says the dates of birth and the ages of Cain and his descendants are unknown.
Abel kneels by his altar with a lamb while Cain stands by his altar of produce.
A colored picture shows Adam and Eve standing under a tree in the Garden of Eden, with the date 4004 B.C. beside them.
"Let there be light," with the Hebrew words, and Genesis 1:27: God created man in his own image, male and female.
Abel is labeled "the first martyr," with his date marked unknown.
The stream of Adam and Eve begins the chart at 4004 B.C. and is marked 930 years, Adam's age at death.
The author explains that time and place are "the two great eyes of history," and that the chart and map are meant to fix both in the mind.
Cain raises a club over Abel, who lies dead beside the altars.

A large map of the Eastern Hemisphere; bright colors mark the lands that were part of recorded history before the discovery of America, such as Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece, Carthage and Asia Minor.
Enoch, second from Adam on Cain's line, branches off Cain's stream with no date given.
Seth, son of Adam, begins at 3874 B.C. (130 A.M.) and lives 912 years. The chart notes that Adam talked with Seth 800 years.

entries.t: Opening note on the chart's dates
entries.p: The chart opens with Genesis 1:1 and says Moses gives no date for the creation. It explains that its dates follow Archbishop Usher's system and counts the Bible's books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 66 in all.
Irad, third from Adam on Cain's line.

A panel says Genesis covers 2369 years, from the Creation to the death of Joseph in 1635 B.C., and sums up chapters 1-3: creation, the Sabbath, the garden of Eden, the naming of the animals, marriage, and the fall and expulsion from Paradise.
A caption says all the history of man before the Flood is found in the first six chapters of Genesis.
Enos, grandson of Adam, begins at 3769 B.C. (235 A.M.) and lives 905 years.
Mehujael, fourth from Adam on Cain's line.
Portrait of the Greek historian Herodotus, born 484 B.C., died about 400 B.C. (time of death uncertain), one of the historians the chart drew on.
Below the time line, a row of names with their ages at their sons' births (Adam 130, Seth 105, Enos 90 and on) is labeled "These lines show the genealogy of Christ."

entries.t: The four women named before the Flood
entries.p: A note says only four women's names survive from before the Flood: Eve, Adah and Zillah (wives of Lamech), and Naamah his daughter, all Cainites except Eve.
Cainan (Kenan), great-grandson of Adam, begins at 3679 B.C. (325 A.M.) and lives 910 years. The chart adds an Arabian tradition that he held a world empire.
A "conjectural" scene of Stone Age life: a woman grinds grain on a stone mill by a fire while a man stands with a club.
Portrait of the Athenian historian Thucydides, born 471 B.C., died 401 B.C.
Methusael (Methushael), fifth from Adam on Cain's line.
Portrait of the Greek writer Xenophon, born about 444 B.C., who lived to about 90.
Drawings of stone and bone tools from Denmark: a stone saw, a dagger, toothed flint spearheads, an axe-hammer, a two-edged axe and a bone comb, shown as the "stone age of man."
Mahalaleel begins at 3609 B.C. (395 A.M.) and lives 895 years.
Portrait of the Roman historian Livy, born 59 B.C., died A.D. 17.
Lamech, sixth from Adam on Cain's line, is called "the first polygamist on record"; his stream splits for his two wives.
A note says that the "creation of the world," or the era Anno Mundi (year of the world), here means only the start of the human race.

The list of sources behind the chart, starting with the Bible and Josephus and including Usher's Annals, Rollin, Rawlinson and Grote. It ends with a note on the Arundel Marbles (Parian Chronicle), found on Paros about 1610.
Portrait of the Roman historian Sallust, born 86 B.C., died 34 B.C.
Jared begins at 3544 B.C. (460 A.M.) and lives 962 years. An Arabian tradition on the chart says he was the first of Seth's line to marry among the Cainites.
Naamah, daughter of Lamech, whose name the chart glosses as "loveliness."
Jabal, son of Lamech and Adah, the father of those who live in tents and keep cattle.
Tubal-cain, son of Lamech by Zillah, is called a maker of every cutting tool of copper and iron and "the Vulcan of the Greeks."
Jubal, son of Lamech and Adah, the father of all who play the harp and organ.
Portrait of the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, born A.D. 23, died A.D. 79.
A panel says the chart uses the era Anno Mundi 4004 before Christ, following Archbishop Usher and the Hebrew Pentateuch, the generally received standard.

A coin of Apamea in Phrygia shows an ark floating on water with a man and woman inside, a dove with a branch on the roof, and the Greek name of Noah. The chart says it was struck under Marcus Aurelius Alexander.
A map of the world as the Hebrews knew it from Genesis 10, with Javan, Gomer, Gog, Tubal, Assyria, Babylon, Elam, Uz, Sheba, Egypt, Ethiopia and Tarshish around "the Sea."
Portrait of the Roman historian Tacitus, born A.D. 58, died A.D. 120.
Portrait of the English historian Edward Gibbon, born 1737, died 1794.
A heading names the Patriarchal Age, from 4004 B.C. to 1491 B.C.
Enoch, "seventh from Adam," begins at 3382 B.C. (622 A.M.) and lives 365 years before God takes him.
A small table compares dates for the Creation: Hebrew Pentateuch 4004 B.C., Samaritan Pentateuch 4700, Septuagint 5872, Talmudists 5344, Josephus 4658 and Dr. Hales 5411.

A drawing of the Rosetta Stone, a black basalt slab found by the French in Egypt in 1799 and now in the British Museum. Its text in hieroglyphics, demotic and Greek praises Ptolemy Epiphanes, about 195 B.C., and gave Champollion the key to hieroglyphics.
A cuneiform inscription from an ancient Chaldean brick, shown reduced. It is read to mean that Urukh, king of Hur and of the land of Akkad, built a temple to Beltis.

entries.t: Stone Age tools found in Switzerland
entries.p: Tools found in Switzerland: hatchet-hammers, hoes or picks of deer horn, bone bodkins or needles, and skewers or pins.
Methuselah, son of Enoch, begins at 3317 B.C. (687 A.M.) and lives 969 years. The chart notes he talked with Adam 243 years.
A panel of quotations on how long passed between the first creation of heaven and earth and the shaping of the world for man, beginning with Genesis 1:1-2.
The pillar Mesha, king of Moab in Ahab's time (900 B.C. on the chart), set up at Dibon; the chart calls its inscription the oldest connected alphabetic writing then known and shows part of it.

entries.t: Note on the Book of Enoch
entries.p: A note says there is a book still in existence called the Book of Enoch, generally thought apocryphal, and perhaps written by a devout Christian of the first century (citing Edward Robinson's Bible dictionary).
A note says Jared was the first of Seth's line to break the command of Enos that forbade marrying the Cainites, a mixing that the note says wore away every moral and religious principle.
A note says an old tradition gave Adam 33 sons and 23 daughters.
Under 'Pictorial Language, 334 B.C.' the chart tells how Darius sent Alexander a bat, a ball and a sack of seeds, and Alexander answered with a bitter wild melon; drawings show each object.

entries.t: Pictorial language: the Scythians answer Darius
entries.p: In 500 B.C. Darius Hystaspes demands earth and water from Scythia; the drawings show the Scythians' answer of a bird, a mouse, a frog and arrows, meaning 'fly, hide, dive, or our arrows are your doom,' and Darius retreats.
A table of Egyptian hieroglyphic signs matched to the letters of the alphabet, 'after Bunsen.'

entries.t: Picture emblems: war, peace, justice, death
entries.p: Drawings show picture-symbols: an arm with a hatchet for war, a pipe of peace, a balance as 'the language of justice,' and a skull and crossbones for death.
A line on Enoch's stream notes his godliness and his being taken by God in Genesis 5:24, and that Jude 14 calls Enoch a prophet.
Lamech's stream begins at his birth in 3130 B.C., the year 874 after Creation, and is labeled with his life span of 777 years.

entries.t: Brother-sister marriage until the law of Moses
entries.p: A note says marriage of brother and sister was common until the law of Moses forbade it in 1491 B.C.

A table compares Hebrew, ancient Phoenician, Greek and Hebrew coin letters; notes say Cadmus brought 15 Phoenician letters to Greece about 1500 B.C., the Greek alphabet had 16 letters until 400 B.C., and a list gives the letter counts of 14 languages.
A panel on Babylon and Assyria: Babylon on the Euphrates and Nineveh on the Tigris, Nimrod founding Babylon and Ashur naming Assyria.
A panel on Greece, the land of orators, poets and heroes, whose history begins with gods and demigods and fades after the fall of the Macedonian empire in 323 B.C.

A panel on Egypt, the early seat of political civilization, dividing its history into three periods: the age of pyramids before Cambyses' conquest in 525 B.C., the Ptolemies, and decline under Muslim rule.
A panel on Phoenicia, the ancient trading people credited with the alphabet; Tyre was 'queen of the seas' until Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it in 572 B.C.
A note says a talent was about 125 pounds troy; a talent of silver was worth about $1,500 and a talent of gold about $24,000.
Adam's stream ends at 3074 B.C., the year 930 after Creation, marked 'Death of Adam.'
On the line of fathers below the axis, Lamech is shown aged 182 when Noah was born.
Two notes quote Josephus: Seth and his descendants were good, virtuous and happy for seven generations, and they invented the study of the heavenly bodies and their order.
Enoch's stream ends at 3017 B.C., the year 987 after Creation, when 'he was not, for God took him.'
A scene of tents, herdsmen, horses and cattle illustrates 'Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle' (Genesis 4:20).

A panel on Persia, anciently called Elam, beginning with Abraham's defeat of its king Chedorlaomer (Genesis 14) and running from Cyrus in 558 B.C. to Alexander, the Parthians and the new Persian kingdom of A.D. 226.
A panel on Rome, from a few miles around its hills to near-universal rule under the Caesars, and its lasting mark on the modern world.
A panel says the early history of India and China long lay in darkness, that India's writings are very large, and that China's civilization has changed little since the Christian era.
A note quoting Dr. Eadie says Mesopotamia, or Padan-aram, between the Tigris and Euphrates, was the first home of man before and after the Flood.
Seth's stream ends at 2962 B.C., the year 1042 after Creation.
A note says the Arabian name of Enoch is Edris, and that their traditions call him an eminent astronomer, mathematician and prophet of God.
Jared's stream is labeled with his life span of 962 years.
Noah's stream branches from Lamech's at 2948 B.C., the year 1056 after Creation, and is labeled with his life span of 950 years.

entries.t: From Adam to Moses in six links
entries.p: A chain of linked bars shows how the story from Creation to the death of Moses, 2553 years, could pass down by word of mouth through overlapping lives: Adam, Methuselah, Shem, Isaac, Levi (with Kohath), Amram and Moses.
A line counts how many years Methuselah lived alongside the earlier fathers: Seth 355 years, Enos 453, Cainan 548, Mahalaleel 603, Jared 735 and Enoch 300.
Isaac is a link in the chain of overlapping lives from Adam to Moses, with the figure 77 years printed between him and Levi.
Titled 'Iron Age from Tubal-cain,' the scene shows the Cainites with a timbrel, a pipe and a harp for Jubal, and Tubal-cain at the anvil, the instructor of every worker in brass and iron.
The stream of Enos ends at 2864 B.C., the year 1140 after Creation.
A panel says the nations of Europe swarmed from Asia, and that about the fourth century A.D. northern tribes overran Germany, Gaul, Britain and Ireland.
Cainan (Kenan) is labeled with his life span of 910 years.
Levi, son of Jacob, is a link in the chain from Adam to Moses, joined to Amram through Kohath.
Mahalaleel's stream is labeled with his life span of 895 years.
Kohath, son of Levi and grandfather of Moses, is drawn as the extra sixth link between Levi and Amram.
Two huge winged bulls with human heads guard a palace gate, captioned '20 ft. long, 20 ft. high.'

entries.t: Sculptures from Nineveh, now in the British Museum
entries.p: A panel says Henry Layard found ten colossal stone bulls at Sennacherib's palace in Nineveh in 1849, two bearing his annals, and quotes his claim to have taken 46 of Hezekiah's cities and shut him up in Jerusalem, matching 2 Kings 18:13-14.
Amram, father of Moses, is the last link before Moses in the chain of overlapping lives.
The chart says Lamech is the first man on record who died a natural death before his father, five years before Methuselah.
Moses ends the chain of links that the chart says carried the history from Creation to his death.
Cainan's stream ends at 2769 B.C., the year 1235 after Creation.
Daggers and swords with bronze handles and iron blades from the tombs at Hallstatt, Austria, discovered by M. Ramsauer.
A panel on the kingdom of the Medes, east of Assyria, which formed the core of the Medo-Persian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 558 B.C.
A line counts how many years Noah lived alongside the earlier fathers: Cainan 179 years, Mahalaleel 234, Jared 366 and Lamech 595.

entries.t: Lamech as a link to Creation
entries.p: A note says Lamech could talk with Adam 56 years and learn the history of the Garden of Eden, and with Shem 98 years, linking Creation to the death of Shem, a period of 2158 years.
Mahalaleel's stream ends at 2714 B.C., the year 1290 after Creation.
Along the time axis the chart quotes Genesis 5:27: 'And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years, and he died.'
The line of fathers says Noah was 502 years old when Shem was born, citing Genesis 5:32.

entries.t: The Seven Wonders of the World
entries.p: A list of the Seven Wonders: the Pyramids, Babylon's walls and gardens, the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, the statue of Jupiter at Olympia, the Mausoleum, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Pharos of Alexandria, with dates and sizes.

entries.t: Traditions about the Tower of Babel
entries.p: A panel gathers old traditions of the Tower of Babel from Abydenus, the Sibyl and Greek fable, and Herodotus' Temple of Belus, which it argues matches Babel in place, material and name.

entries.t: Iron tools from a Swiss lake
entries.p: A sickle, an iron hatchet with a square socket and a lance-head found in a lake in Switzerland.

entries.t: Years of history in the Old Testament
entries.p: A panel counts 3607 years of history in the Old Testament: 2369 years in Genesis and 1238 years in the other 38 books.

A text block tells the Flood: the ark finished in 2348 B.C. (with a question mark), Noah's family entering in his six hundredth year, the ark resting on Ararat, the mountaintops seen, and the family leaving the ark in 2347 B.C.
Jared's stream ends at 2582 B.C., the year 1422 after Creation.

A man hollows out a log boat with fire while others pole a canoe; the text says the first floating craft in history was Noah's ark and gives dates for early ships and the Argonaut expedition, 1263 B.C.
A woman spins thread from fiber tied to a tree while another weaves at a simple wooden loom.

entries.t: Lamech dies five years before the Flood
entries.p: Lamech's stream is labeled again with his 777 years and the note that he died five years before the Flood.
Methuselah's stream is labeled with his 969 years and the note that he died in the year of the Flood, before it came.
Noah's stream is labeled again with his 950 years, noting that he had three sons only.

entries.t: God commands Noah to build the ark
entries.p: Quoting 'The earth was corrupt and filled with violence' (Genesis 6:11), the chart dates God's command to Noah to build an ark to 2466 B.C. with a question mark.

entries.t: Noah, his three sons, and their posterity
entries.p: A table of the 'probable destinations' of Noah's family: the sons of Shem, Ham and Japheth, each paired with the nations the chart says came from them.
A note says eight souls were saved from the old world 'which perished' to fill the new world: Noah, Shem, Ham, Japheth and their four wives.
A note says Noah and his family were in the ark one year and ten days, entering in 2348 B.C. and leaving in 2347 B.C.
A farm scene of women and children working with grain and a mortar, captioned "Agriculture during iron age." A note above it tells the old stories of who first taught spinning.

entries.t: Pillars of Methuselah, Noah and Shem
entries.p: A stone pillar and a brick pillar with figures beside them. The caption, citing Josephus, says that the year before the Flood the history and discoveries of the world were written on two pillars, which still stood in Moses' time.
Ham, Noah's "younger son" (Genesis 9:24), born 2443 B.C. by the chart, who had four sons.
Japheth, Noah's son, called "the elder" (Genesis 10:21), whose line is drawn branching to his seven sons.
Shem, born 2446 B.C., who lived 600 years. The chart notes he was 98 at the Flood, had five sons, and talked with Methuselah 98 years.

A table of the dates different authorities give for the Flood, from 2348 B.C. (Ussher and the English Bible) to 3246 B.C. (the Septuagint), including the Hebrew Bible, Playfair, Clinton, the Samaritan Pentateuch, Josephus and Dr. Hales.

entries.t: The Ark resting on Ararat, under the rainbow
entries.p: Noah's ark sits on a mountaintop under a rainbow, with the river valley below; the chart gives the ark's size (300 by 50 by 30 cubits, 547 by 91 by 54 feet, 81,000 tons) and quotes God's promise of the rainbow from Genesis 9.
Arphaxad, son of Shem, born 2346 B.C., who lived 438 years. The chart notes he talked with Abraham 88 years.

Five portraits that sort humanity into the races used by 19th-century writers: "Negro or African," "European or Caucasian," "Malay," "Indian or American" and "Chinese or Mongolian." It reflects the race theories of the chart's own day.
The Flood is dated 2348 B.C., "2348 years to the birth of Christ" (1656 years from Creation by the chart's axis), and the lines of Japheth's sons begin.

entries.t: The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Phut and Canaan
entries.p: Ham's sons Cush, Mizraim, Phut and Canaan; the chart notes that Mizraim "settles Egypt."
Salah, son of Arphaxad, born 2311 B.C., who lived 433 years and, the chart says, talked with Abraham 118 years.

entries.t: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Lud and Aram
entries.p: Shem's sons Elam, Asshur, Lud and Aram, with the note that Asshur "builded Nineveh" (Genesis 10:11).

A tall stepped tower captioned "The Tower of Babel, or Temple of Jupiter Belus." The text beside it says it was the temple Herodotus saw in Babylon, a quarter mile square at the base and 650 feet high in eight stories, later despoiled by Xerxes.
Eber (Heber), born 2281 B.C., who lived 464 years. The chart says he had two sons, one of them Peleg, and outlived Abraham four years.
Japheth's seven sons: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras.

entries.t: The descendants of Noah spread over the earth
entries.p: "The descendants of Noah disperse over the earth about 2247 B.C.": Shem's probably in Asia, Ham's probably in Africa, Japheth's probably in Europe.
Nimrod, son of Cush, "founds Babylon"; the chart quotes Genesis 10 on the mighty hunter whose kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar.

entries.t: Sidon and Heth, sons of Canaan
entries.p: Canaan's sons: Sidon, his firstborn, who "founds Sidon" (the Sidonians and Amorites are noted), and Heth.

entries.t: Confusion of tongues and dispersion, 2247 B.C.
entries.p: "101 years to the 'Confusion of Tongues' and 'Dispersion,' 2247 B.C."
Peleg, son of Eber, born 2247 B.C., who lived 239 years; "in his days was the earth divided" (Genesis 10:25).
Joktan, Peleg's brother, who "had 13 sons" (Genesis 10:26-30).
Reu, son of Peleg, born 2217 B.C., who lived 239 years.

"The descendants of Canaan settle Phoenicia or Canaan... but its history is almost unknown." Beside it, Tyre's conquerors are listed: Nebuchadnezzar 572 B.C., Cyrus 537, Alexander 332, Rome 47 B.C. and the Turks A.D. 1516.

entries.t: Egypt: Mizraim or Menes settles Egypt
entries.p: The stream of Egypt begins: "Mizraim or Menes, descendant of Ham, settles Egypt and builds Thebes."

"Chaldaea or Babylon": Nimrod "subverts the patriarchal government and establishes the regal, and founds the kingdom of Babylon on the Euphrates, 2245 B.C.," reigning 121 years; after death he was deified as Orion.

entries.t: China founded by Fohi or Yao
entries.p: The yellow stream of China: "founded by Fohi or Yao, supposed to be the Noah of the Bible," with the 1st dynasty, Hiah. The chart says Chinese historians date him 2240 B.C. and credit him with symbolic writing, music, dress and sacrifice at the solstices.
Serug, son of Reu, born 2185 B.C., who lived 230 years.

The Roman goddess Juno seated on a throne, captioned "Juno, Queen of Heaven, the sister and wife of Jupiter." The chart notes that it uses the Greek names for the kings and gods of Babylon and Assyria.

entries.t: Greece: Javan settles Greece or Ionia
entries.p: "Greece (Attica, Arcadia, Sparta)": "Javan or Ion settles Greece or Ionia."
A camp of cone-shaped tents with people walking among them, showing the tent life of the early generations after the Flood.

entries.t: Sidon founded by Sidon, son of Canaan
entries.p: A walled city by the water, captioned "Sidon founded by Sidon son of Canaan, at a very early and uncertain period" (Joshua 19:28).
Nahor, son of Serug, born 2155 B.C., who lived 148 years.
Figures in Chaldean dress, one seated on a throne, from "the most ancient records of Chaldaea." The text beside it says the monuments give only a very scanty account of how the Chaldeans lived.

"'Babylon the great' for some 1700 years stood as the queen city of the world": its walls 300 feet high and 75 feet wide enclosed 225 square miles, with brazen gates, quays, temples and artificial mountains and lakes. It was conquered by Cyrus 538 B.C., Darius 518, Alexander 331 and later Demetrius, Trajan and Omar.

entries.t: The Assyrian Empire does not begin until 1300 B.C.
entries.p: A heading that says "The Assyrian Empire does not begin until 1300 B.C." (Rawlinson).

entries.t: Jupiter, father of gods and men
entries.p: Jupiter enthroned with a scepter, thunderbolt and eagle, captioned "Jupiter, who was the father of Gods and men."

entries.t: Greek beginnings: the Fabulous and Heroic Ages
entries.p: Says the Greeks are thought to descend from Javan, son of Japheth, and divides early Greek history into the "Fabulous Age" to the Trojan war (1184 B.C.), the "Heroic Age," "Traditionary History" and "Authentic History" from 490 B.C.; the Pelasgi held Greece before Inachus, Cecrops, Cadmus and Pelops arrived.

A note that dates the battle of the nine kings to 1913 B.C. and answers "Who was Melchizedek of Genesis 14 and Hebrews 7?" with "probably Shem," who was still living, the oldest father, and king and priest of his tribe.
"Assyria": Asshur, 88, "founds Nineveh on the Tigris," later conquered by Ninus (Genesis 10:11).
"2111, Thebes built by Busiris (Ussher)," on the line of Egypt's early kings.
Belus, 55 years, on the chart's line of the kings of Babylon, starting 2124.
Osymandyas, an early king on the chart's line of Egypt, with the note that his victories in Asia were commemorated in sculpture and painting.
Terah, born 2126 B.C., who lived 205 years and begat Haran, Nahor and Abram; he died in Haran when Abraham was 75.
Neptune, crowned and holding a trident, rising from a shell, captioned "Neptune, Brother of Jupiter."
"Sicyon founded by Aegialus."
"Hyksos Kings, 2080-1820" (from Blair), the foreign Shepherd Kings of Egypt, whose time the chart also calls uncertain.

entries.t: Terah, Abram and Lot leave Ur
entries.p: Terah, Abram and his wife, Nahor and Lot leave Ur for Canaan and come to Haran (Padan-Aram); Terah dies there, and Abram and Lot go on into Canaan in 1921 B.C.

entries.t: Costumes of the priests of Babylon
entries.p: Robed priests in tall headdresses praying before a small shrine, with a star and crescent moon above, labeled "Costumes of Priests of Babylon."
Massive sloping Egyptian temple gateways and an obelisk, labeled "Ancient Egyptian Architecture."
"Ninus, 52, son, conquers Assyria, enlarges and improves his kingdom by the assistance of his noble queen Semiramis, who succeeds him."
"Aesculapius, the Greek god of medicine": his worship came to Rome in 291 B.C., and his priests, the Asclepiadae, practiced medicine.
A harbor city with a bridge, towers and sailing ships, captioned "City of Tyre was founded at a very early date" (Joshua 19:29).
Vulcan the smith with a hammer at his anvil, captioned "Vulcan, Son of Juno."
Haran, born 2056 B.C. by the chart, who "died in Ur of the Chaldees, in the land of his nativity, before his father" (Genesis 11:28).
Uchoris, the Egyptian king who "builds Memphis" on the chart's line of kings.
Nahor, Terah's son and Abraham's brother, whose line leads to Bethuel and Rebekah.

"Semiramis, 42, wife," under whom Babylon was enlarged and beautified as the capital of her empire; she invades Libya, Ethiopia and India in 1973, and a note says she was later worshipped as "the celestial Venus."
"1998, Noah dies."

A table of Egypt's dynasties and kings from Manetho and the Table of Abydos, from Khufu (Cheops) who built the Great Pyramid to Egypt's conquest by Persia in 525 B.C., noting Shishak (Sheshonk) and the Hyksos.
Iscah, daughter of Haran.

entries.t: Map of the valley of the Nile
entries.p: A small drawing of the Nile winding past pyramids, with Memphis, Thebes and "Valley of the Nile" labeled.
A centaur, half man and half horse, drawing a bow, one of the creatures of Greek myth.

entries.t: Milcah, niece and wife to Nahor
entries.p: Milcah, Haran's daughter, "niece and wife to Nahor."
Two women in long robes beside date palms and a bird, labeled "Babylonian Women with dates."
"Ninyas, son, 38": Nineveh is seized by the Arabs and the empire divided into four kingdoms, 1937.

entries.t: Sarah, sister and wife to Abraham
entries.p: Sarah, "sister and wife to Abraham"; her death is marked at 1859 B.C.

entries.t: The call of Abram and the covenant
entries.p: "1921, the call of Abram": he and Lot settle at Shechem; a famine drives them into Egypt in 1919; they return in 1917 and separate in 1916; in 1898 the promise is renewed, circumcision is given as "the sign and seal," and Abram and Sarai are renamed Abraham and Sarah.
Lot, Haran's son and Abraham's nephew (Genesis 19), whose two daughters' lines branch from his.
A note that China's claims to great age reflect the Patriarchal Age, and that Shem, Noah, Methuselah and Adam may have furnished the foundation for its traditional history.

entries.t: India: Brahma, the Vedas and the Puranas
entries.p: A long line of text: an eclipse of the sun observed by Chinese astronomers in 2155 B.C., the worship of Brahma in India about 2000 B.C., Sanskrit as the sacred language, and the Vedas and Puranas, known only to a few learned men of the higher castes.
"Shin-Nong, 146," who taught farming and how to make bread from rice; the chart suggests he was "perhaps the Shem of the Bible."
Hagar, Sarah's servant, the mother of Ishmael.
Fire falls on the cities while Lot and his two daughters escape and Lot's wife stands behind them, captioned "Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed 1898" and "Lot and his 2 daughters escape."
The kings of Genesis 14: Babylon or Shinar (Amraphel), Assyria or Ellasar (Arioch), Syria or Goim (Tidal) and Persia or Elam (Chedorlaomer), with "the 5 cities of the plain subdued."
A mermaid holding a mirror and combing her hair as she rises from the water.

entries.t: Abram goes down to Egypt in the famine
entries.p: A line marked "1920, a famine drives Abram to Egypt" turns down into the Egyptian stream and back up with "Abraham returns."
Abram, then Abraham, born 1996 B.C., who lived 175 years; the chart calls him "the father of the faithful" and "the friend of God" and notes the family lived in Canaan from 1921 to 1706 B.C.
A shield with crossed swords and spears, captioned "Battle of the Nine Kings, 1913," Genesis 14.
Bethuel, son of Nahor and "cousin of Isaac," father of Rebekah and Laban.
"Pharaoh," the king of Egypt when Abram went down in the famine of 1920 B.C.

entries.t: Abraham and Lot separate; Lot taken captive
entries.p: "1916, Abraham and Lot separate. 1913, Elamite invasion. Lot and all of Sodom taken captive by Chedorlaomer. Abraham pursued and recaptured all and slew the 4 kings."
Ishmael, born 1910 B.C., who lived 137 years and "begat 12 sons, princes"; the chart calls him the father of the tribes of the Arabs.
An Egyptian temple gateway with two obelisks and seated statues, with riders passing by, labeled "Thebes."
Rebekah, "2nd cousin and wife to Isaac." A note says Isaac married her at 40 and at 137 sent Jacob into Mesopotamia, 600 miles.
Keturah, "Abraham's 2nd wife," who had six children.

entries.t: Abraham's trial: the offering of Isaac
entries.p: Abraham leans over Isaac, who lies bound on a stone altar, captioned "1871. Abraham's Trial."
Moab, son of Lot's elder daughter, "Father of the Moabites" (Genesis 19:37).

entries.t: Isaac offered; Sarah's death; Keturah's sons
entries.p: "1871, Isaac offered on Mt. Moriah. 1859, death of Sarah, aged 127 years. 1853, Abraham married Keturah," who bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah, ancestors of many Arabian tribes.
The stream of Persia, with Jemshid and Feridun, and the note that Iran's title of "Schah," or king, is still kept by the kings of Persia.
Men in Greek and Egyptian dress work and talk together, captioned "Inachus from Phoenicia founds Argos" and "First immigration into Greece by Inachus 1856."
Ben-Ammi, son of Lot's younger daughter, "Father of the Ammonites" (Genesis 19:38).

Dates different scholars give for Menes, Egypt's first king (from 2691 to 5004 B.C.), the causes of this disagreement, and "Egypt's three empires according to Rawlinson": Old, Middle (Hyksos or Shepherd) and New.
Laban, Rebekah's brother, whose line runs on toward Jacob's wives Leah and Rachel.
Apophis, a king on the line of Egypt's rulers before Joseph's time.

entries.t: "I seek a bride for my master": Rebekah at the well
entries.p: Abraham's servant with his camels meets Rebekah at the well, captioned "I seek a bride for my master," "Rebekah 1856" and "Isaac's servant."
Esau, Jacob's twin brother, "father of the Edomites." The chart notes that at forty he took two Canaanite wives, a grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
The head of the Great Sphinx, labeled "Great Sphinx" and "Antedates the Pyramids," with its measurements: 56 feet from breast to head, a head 28 feet around, and 128 feet long.
Jacob, born 1836 B.C., who lived 147 years; his name was changed to Israel in 1751 B.C. by the chart.
Whang-Ti, who "spoke as soon as weaned, became emperor at 12 years of age," discovered the use of the magnet and made many inventions, according to Chinese history.
Men in short kilts work the ground with hoes and an ox-drawn plow, a scene of Egyptian farm life in the time of Abraham and Isaac.
Isaac, born 1896 B.C., who lived 180 years.
"Amenophis I, working in gold and silver mines, 1806."

entries.t: Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah
entries.p: Abraham buys a field and the cave of Machpelah near Mamre (now Hebron) for a family tomb, weighing out 400 shekels of silver "current money with the merchant" (Genesis 23).

entries.t: Esau's wives: Judith, Bashemath and Mahalath
entries.p: Esau's wives Judith and Bashemath (Genesis 26:34) and Mahalath, "cousin and wife to Esau" (Genesis 28:9).
Leah, "4th cousin and wife to Jacob," who had six sons and one daughter.
Jacob sleeps on the ground while angels go up and down a ladder to heaven, captioned "Jacob's Ladder," Genesis 28:12, 1779.
"1st Book, Genesis, embraces 2369 years of history,"
Rachel, Jacob's wife, who had two sons; her death is marked at 1732 B.C. (Genesis 35:19).
Rocks and rough water, with the labels "Ogyges, King of Boeotia" and "Deluge in Attica 1764." The text says the flood laid Attica waste for nearly 200 years.
Phoroneus, 60 years, king of Argos after Inachus; a note says he brought in the practice of offering sacrifices to the gods in 1773.
Bilhah, who had two sons, and Zilpah, the servants who bore sons to Jacob.
"1st Reuben," who had four sons (Genesis 46:9).
"Of Jacob's children and grandchildren 66 went down to Egypt, and the 9 wives of his sons made 'threescore and fifteen souls'" (Acts 7:14; Genesis 46:26).
"2nd Simeon," who had six sons.

Quotes Rawlinson that the vast ages claimed by Babylonians, Assyrians, Hindus and Chinese are fiction, and that their reliable history starts much later (Babylon about 2300 B.C., Assyria about 1500 B.C.).

A table after Rawlinson of the dates of early civilizations: the Septuagint's Flood 3200 B.C., Egypt 2450, Babylon 2300, Asia Minor 2000, Phoenicia 1550, Assyria 1500, Iran and India about 1500-1200, Greece 1200, Phrygia and Lydia 900, Etruria 650 and Lycia 600.
Jacob stands by the stone he set up and anointed, captioned "Bethel, House of God," Genesis 28:18.
The pyramids, captioned "Great Pyramid near Gizeh, date uncertain," 461 feet high and 476 square, covering 12 acres. A note sends the reader to the 20th century B.C. column for its builders.
"3rd Levi," who had three sons and from whom came the Levitical priesthood.
"9th Dan," who had one son (Genesis 46:23).
"10th Naphtali," who had four sons.
"4th Judah," whose line leads on through Pharez; the chart notes he had three sons.
"11th Joseph," born 1745 B.C. by the chart, who lived 110 years.
Dinah, Jacob's daughter by Leah.
A stream marked "Joseph sold into Egypt, aged 17, 1728" runs down into the Egyptian kings.
"7th Gad," who had seven sons.
"6th Zebulun," who had three sons.
"2nd Dynasty, Shang," beginning in 1756 on the chart's China stream.
Simeon's six sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul.
Reuben's four sons: Hanoch, Phallu, Hezron and Carmi.
Joseph lies asleep under the sun, moon and stars, while sheaves of grain bow down to one sheaf, captioned "Joseph's Dream."
"5th Issachar," who had four sons.
"Joseph made governor of Egypt, 1715 B.C."
"Pharaoh, King," the ruler of Egypt when Joseph was made governor.
"8th Asher," who had four sons and one daughter (Serah).
"12th Benjamin, the youngest," who had ten sons (Genesis 46:21).

entries.t: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath and Merari
entries.p: Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath (who lived 133 years) and Merari, with the note "From Levi came the Levitical priesthood."

entries.t: Lydia and Phrygia in Asia Minor
entries.p: The stream of "Lydia and Phrygia in Asia Minor" begins, under the Atyadaen kings, first dynasty.
Judah's twin sons Pharez, who had two sons, and Zarah; Pharez carries the line toward Christ.

entries.t: Jacob and his family go into Egypt, 1706 B.C.
entries.p: "Jacob and family go into Egypt, 1706 B.C.," which the heading reckons as 642 years after the Flood and 215 years after the call of Abraham.
Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 50:23) with their sons Machir, Peresh, Shuthelah and Bered, noted from 1 Chronicles 7.
Joash son of Ahaziah, reigning 39 years: good, then evil, and slain.
Jehoahaz son of Jehu on the kingdom of Israel's stream, reigning 16 years.

entries.t: Kings of Israel and Judah in the cuneiform inscriptions
entries.p: A list of Israelite and Judean kings named on Assyrian inscriptions, with their Assyrian spellings, among them Ahab, Jehu, Menahem, Hoshea, Ahaz, Hezekiah and Manasseh.
A large catapult, drawn under the reign of Uzziah, who the Bible says made machines to shoot arrows and large stones.
Shalmaneser II of Assyria (in the chart's numbering), reigning 37 years.
Two short notes: Zerubbabel's Temple, built 535-515 BC and profaned by Antiochus Epiphanes, and Herod's Temple, rebuilt by Herod and destroyed by the Romans in AD 70.

A text panel on Solomon's Temple: its size in cubits and its history from 1004 BC to 588 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar plundered and destroyed it. It lists its founding in 1012 BC, dedication in 1004 BC and the times it was plundered or repaired.

Labels for the 13th and 14th books: 1 Chronicles, a genealogical history from the Creation to the death of David (1015 BC), and 2 Chronicles, from David's death to the captivity by Nebuchadnezzar in 588 BC, 427 years.
Dido, sister of Pygmalion, comes from Tyre and founds Carthage; she bought as much land as a bull's hide could enclose and cut the hide into a very fine string.
Ben-hadad, king of Syria (Aram), on the Syrian stream.
Assyrian archers in the time of Sennacherib, one drawing a bow beside a soldier with a shield.
The chart's heading for 2 Kings, the 12th book of the Bible, which tells of the kings of Israel and Judah down to the fall of Jerusalem.
Jehoash (Joash) of Israel, reigning 16 years.
Romulus and Remus nursed by a she-wolf.
Amaziah of Judah, reigning 29 years, 'fair reign', and slain.
Jonah, the 32nd book, 4 chapters.
Jeroboam II of Israel, with a reign of 41 years, the longest in the northern kingdom.
Bocchoris 'the wise', a king of Egypt, reigning 44 years by the chart.
Vul-Nirari III, whom the chart equates with Pul, ruling with his son 781-773 BC.
Joel, the 29th book, 3 chapters, dated 800 BC.
The label of Athens and its archons.
Amos, the 30th book, 9 chapters, dated 784 BC.
Uzziah of Judah, reigning 52 years; the chart says 'he did right' and that he died of leprosy.
Menahem bribes Pul, king of Assyria, to leave with 1,000 talents of silver in 770 BC.
The label of China's stream of kings.
A siege machine labeled 'Crow', a swinging beam set against a tower.
The label where Babylon's stream begins, with Belesis, 28 years.
Menahem of Israel, reigning 11 years.

entries.t: Zechariah and Shallum, kings of Israel
entries.p: Two short reigns noted in slanting letters: Zechariah for six months and Shallum for one month.
Hosea, the 28th book, a prophet active for about 60 years (785-725 BC), sent to rebuke Israel for its sins and idolatry and to warn Judah.
Pekahiah of Israel, reigning 2 years.
Isaiah, the 23rd book, 66 chapters; the prophet's ministry is shown as about 62 years, starting in 760 BC.
A man plowing the furrow for the city wall, and 'April 21st, 753, Rome founded'.
Runners in a race for the first Olympiad, July 1, 776 BC, and the fourth year of the sixth Olympiad.

entries.t: Assyrian library at Calah and Nineveh
entries.p: A note on the Assyrian library: Tiglath-Pileser II, Sargon, Sennacherib and Esarhaddon had inscriptions, astrological texts and histories copied, and the library was moved from Calah to Nineveh.
Pekah of Israel, reigning 20 years and slain. A note beneath says Rome was built in the sixth year of his reign.
The label of Lydia of Asia Minor, Sardis its capital.
Jotham of Judah, reigning 16 years; 'did right'.
Two figures labeled 'Ancient Persian soldier' and 'Ancient Median', one with a spear and round shield.
The chart notes the sun dial of Ahaz in 713 BC, the sign given to Hezekiah when the shadow went back.
So or Sabacon, ruling 50 years, chieftain of a great horde of Ethiopians who took Egypt; a note says Hoshea sent messengers to So in 724 BC.
Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria, reigning 18 years.
Micah, the 33rd book, 7 chapters; the prophet's ministry is shown as 48 years.
Samaria is resettled by Shalmaneser with Cuthaeans, people brought in from elsewhere.
Nabonassar, whose era begins February 26, 747 BC.
Ahaz of Judah, reigning 16 years; 'did not right'.
Romulus, first king of Rome, 38 years.
After a time marked 'Anarchy', Hoshea reigns 9 years, and the stream of Israel ends in 721 BC.
Shalmaneser (IV in the chart's numbering), printed up the Assyrian stream.
Sargon, king of Assyria.
Hezekiah 'the good', reigning 28 years.
Merodach-Baladan of Babylon, 12 years; the chart notes the kingdom was then depressed for several short reigns.
The label of Macedon, whose stream begins with Caranus, who founds Macedon in 813 BC.
Nahum, the 34th book, 3 chapters, dated 700 BC.
'Carried away by Shalmaneser into Assyria, never to return': the chart calls them the lost tribes and marks the end of the kingdom of Israel in 721 BC.
Croesus fears the rising power of Cyrus and marches against him with 420,000 men and 60,000 horse, but is defeated and taken in 546 BC; Cyrus had 196,000 men.
Sennacherib, reigning 24 years.
A covered battering ram on wheels.
Tirhakah, king of Egypt, reigning 20 years.
Numa Pompilius, 42 years, 'a virtuous and religious king'.

entries.t: Shalmaneser's invasions and the fall of Samaria
entries.p: A list of dates: Shalmaneser's invasion 728, Hoshea made to pay tribute, Hoshea revolts 725, Assyrian invasion 724, and Samaria taken in 721 BC.
Esarhaddon, reigning 13 years.
Media revolts; the label of Media's stream, with Deioces, 53 years, king of Media and Persia.
Manasseh 'the wicked', reigning 55 years, which the chart calls the longest Jewish reign.
A movable siege tower on wheels.
A note that different dates are given for the 'eclipse of Thales' (610-585 BC), which separated the Medes and Lydians in a battle on the river Halys.
Solon and Aesop standing before Croesus on his throne.

The statue of Nebuchadnezzar's dream (603 BC): head of gold for Babylon, chest and arms of silver for Medo-Persia, belly and thighs of brass for Alexander's empire, legs of iron for Rome, and feet of iron and clay for Rome broken into ten kingdoms.
Byzantium founded by Byzas, 667 or 715 BC.

Jeremiah weeping in sackcloth. The text beside it tells how Daniel, the princes and the craftsmen were carried away to Babylon, and how Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem in 599 BC and took King Jehoiachin and the temple vessels.
Sardanapalus, the last great king on the Assyrian stream, 43 years.
The label of Egypt's stream of kings.
Amon of Judah, who 'did evil', reigning 2 years from 643 BC.
Zephaniah, the 36th book, 3 chapters, dated 630 BC.
Two Scythian warriors; the caption says the Scythians of the north defeated Cyrus under their queen Tomyris in 529 BC.
Josiah, 'noble king', reigning 31 years.
Lamentations, the 25th book, dated 588 BC.

entries.t: Jehoiakim in chains; seventy years' captivity begins
entries.p: Jehoiakim is taken in chains to Babylon with many captives, Daniel among them, and the 70 years of captivity begin in 606 BC.
Draco and his 'bloody laws', 621 BC.
A note: 561, murder of Holofernes by Judith.
Sappho, Greek poetess.
The fight between the three Horatii and the three Curiatii, 670 BC: one survives, all the others killed.

entries.t: Nabopolassar and the fall of Nineveh
entries.p: Nabopolassar, 21 years: the Babylonian general unites with Cyaxares king of Media, overthrows Sarakas and destroys Nineveh in 610 BC.
Thales, first of the seven sages, who suggests the earth is round.
Cyaxares, king of Media, 40 years.
Pharaoh Necho, reigning 16 years, defeated by Nebuchadnezzar.
Jeremiah, the 24th book, 52 chapters; the prophet is shown as active 40 years from 629 BC.
Jehoahaz son of Josiah, who reigned 3 months.
Jehoiakim, reigning 11 years.
Habakkuk, the 35th book, 3 chapters, placed in the time of Jehoiakim.
The label for the seven wise men of Greece.
Jehoiachin, who reigned 3 months before being taken to Babylon.
Zedekiah, last king of Judah, reigning 11 years.
Ezekiel, the 26th book, 48 chapters; the prophet is shown as active 21 years from 595 BC.
A large gold-colored head of Nebuchadnezzar on the Babylonian stream, 43 years, with the quotations 'the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency' and 'thou art this head of gold'.
Apries or Pharaoh Hophra, reigning 24 years.
At 588 BC (586 by Hales) the chart notes the end of Jewish independence: after this the Jews are under Babylon, Persia, Egypt, Syria and Rome until AD 70, when they were scattered.

Daniel, the 27th book, 12 chapters, written in Babylon; the prophet is shown as active 72 years (606-534 BC). A note says the book is in Chaldee (Aramaic) from chapter 2 verse 4 to the end of chapter 7.
Obadiah, the 31st book, 1 chapter, dated 587 BC with Jeremiah.
The label of the Chaldee-Babylonian Empire, with the 70 years' captivity marked 606 to 536 BC.
A statue on a pedestal for the golden image Nebuchadnezzar set up.
The decree to rebuild Jerusalem was issued by Cyrus in 536 BC.
The label of Carthage; its stream reads that in 550 BC the republic was established, with a first alliance with Rome in 503 BC.
Evil-Merodach and Neriglissar printed up the Babylonian stream between Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus.

entries.t: Jerusalem taken and the temple burnt
entries.p: Jerusalem taken, the temple burnt, walls and city destroyed; Zedekiah's eyes put out, and he and thousands taken captive to Babylon, 588 BC.
Salathiel (Shealtiel) on the line of Jesus' ancestors below the time line.
The Temple of Diana (Artemis) at Ephesus, the third wonder of the world, built in 552 BC and burned on the night Alexander was born, 356 BC.
A portrait of Solon, the Athenian lawgiver.
Nabonidus with 'Belshazzar, son' printed beside him, 18 years, from 556 to 538 BC, when the Babylonian empire ends.

Checkered squares illustrating Pythagoras of Magna Graecia, who the chart says discovered the 47th problem (of Euclid) and the multiplication table and suggested the idea later developed by Copernicus.
585 to 572 BC: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Tyre; the Tyrians abandon their city and move to the island Tyre, which rises to power.
Darius the Mede, or Cyaxares, from 538 BC.
Cyrus or Kaikhosru, 30 years, on the Persian stream.
Belshazzar's feast: Daniel reads the writing on the wall, 'Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin', while Cyrus and his army enter the city through the riverbed, the king is slain and Babylon falls.
The label of Greece's stream.
Haggai, the 37th book (2 chapters, 520 BC), and Zechariah, the 38th book (14 chapters).
Zerubbabel the governor on the Jewish leaders' stream after the return; his name also appears on the line of Jesus' ancestors above.
Cambyses, son of Cyrus, printed up the Persian stream.

entries.t: Daniel's first vision: the lion with eagle's wings
entries.p: A winged lion for Daniel's first beast, which the chart explains as Babylon, quick and strong in conquering Syria, Phoenicia, Judea and Egypt.
Confucius (Kung-fu-tse), 83 years; a note says in 522 BC he remodels the sacred books of the Chinese.

entries.t: Pisistratus and the first public library
entries.p: Pisistratus, who seized power at Athens, founded the first public library there in 544 BC and collected the poems of Homer.
The rape of Lucretia; the Tarquins expelled; the Republic of Rome begins, 509 BC.
A small bust of Psammetichus, king of Egypt, drawn from a statue.
Marathon, September 28, 490 BC: Darius against Miltiades, Aristides and Themistocles.
Darius I Hystaspes, or Gushtasp, 36 years.
Jeshua (Joshua), the high priest of the return.
Ezra, the 15th book, 10 chapters, covering about 80 years (536-456 BC). A note says parts of Ezra are written in Chaldee (Aramaic).

Zerubbabel sent up by Cyrus in 536 BC with 42,360 people to rebuild the Temple; Ezra sent up in the 7th year of Artaxerxes Longimanus; Nehemiah in the 20th year, governor 12 years, rebuilds the walls.

entries.t: Daniel's seventy weeks dated from Ezra
entries.p: In 458 BC Ezra goes up to Jerusalem; the chart notes that some date Daniel's 'seventy weeks' (490 years) from this year.
A bear with three ribs in its mouth, which the chart explains as Medo-Persia with Babylon, Egypt and Lydia.
Abiud on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Aeschylus, the dramatist, who wrote 70 tragedies (7 survive); the chart says he was killed by a tortoise dropped by an eagle.
Gautama (Sakya Muni) Buddha, about 550 BC.

entries.t: Daniel cast into the lions' den
entries.p: A note under the bear dates Daniel's being thrown into the lions' den to 554 BC.

A note on the Samaritans: after the ten tribes were carried away, Samaria was settled with Cuthites and others; when the returning Jews refused their help to rebuild the Temple, the feud began, so the Jews had no dealings with them. Haggai and Zechariah urged the Jews on with the work.
Xerxes, son of Darius, from 485 BC, succeeded by Artabanus.
Joiakim, high priest after Jeshua.
Thermopylae, August 7-9, 480 BC: Xerxes against Leonidas and his brave 300, slain.
The label of the Persian Empire's stream, 559 to 330 BC.
Esther, the 17th book, 10 chapters, covering 12 years.
Ezra as governor, with 'Ezra sent up' printed down the stream.
A bird's-eye view of Babylon, 15 miles square, with the Temple of Jupiter Belus; the walls are 350 feet high, 87 feet thick, with 25 brass gates on each side.
Ahasuerus on his throne with Queen Esther; the caption says Vashti was divorced and Esther made queen, and names the king as Xerxes or Artaxerxes Longimanus.
Pericles, 40 years, 'the greatest of Athenian statesmen'.
Eliakim on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Nehemiah's name printed down the stream of the Jewish leaders.
The ram of Daniel 8:3 with two horns labeled Persia and Media.
Artaxerxes I Longimanus, 40 years.
Hippocrates, 'the father of medicine'.
Nehemiah, the 16th book, 13 chapters, 445 to 433 BC.

entries.t: End of the 39 books of the Old Testament
entries.p: The chart marks the end of the 39 books of the Old Testament at 397 BC, year 3607 from Creation.
Herodotus, 'father of history'.
Eliashib the high priest.
Socrates in prison drinking the hemlock, 399 BC, with weeping friends around him.
Darius II Nothus, 19 years.
The chart notes a temple on Mount Gerizim in 408 BC, built by permission of Darius.
The Parthenon, temple of Minerva at Athens, 442 BC, built by Pericles.
Malachi, the 39th and last book of the Old Testament, 4 chapters, 420 to 397 BC, 23 years.

entries.t: Xerxes reviews his army at the Hellespont
entries.p: Xerxes reviewing his army and navy at the Hellespont, said by Herodotus to be 5,000,000 in 480 BC; soldiers and ships crossing a bridge.
The seated statue of Jupiter (Zeus) Olympius, the fourth wonder, at Olympia, 433 BC, of gold and ivory by Phidias.
Joiada (Jehoiada) the high priest.
Xenophon, who lived 90 years.
Artaxerxes II Mnemon, 'memory', 46 years.
Azor on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Cunaxa in Babylonia, 401 BC: Cyrus defeated and killed by Artaxerxes; the retreat of the 10,000.
390 BC: at the Allia in Italy the Romans are defeated by the Gauls, who then enter and burn Rome.
A portrait bust of Plato.
Aristotle, 62 years, tutor of Alexander.
John (Johanan) the high priest.
Alexander the Great on a rearing horse.
The goat with one great horn, labeled Alexander, that came from the west without touching the ground and struck the ram.
Philip II, 23 years; married first Olympias, second Cleopatra.
Artaxerxes III Ochus.
Chaeronea, 338 BC: Philip defeats the Athenians.
Granicus, May 22, 334 BC.
Issus, 333 BC: Alexander defeats Darius.
Demosthenes declaiming on the seashore.
Arbela, October 1, 331 BC.
The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the fifth wonder, 350 BC.
Jaddua the high priest, in office in the time of Alexander.
Darius III or Codomanus, 6 years, the last on the Persian stream.
Diogenes the Cynic philosopher of Athens sitting in his tub.
Sadoc (Zadok) on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
The red stream of the Macedonian Empire under Alexander III, which swallows the other kingdoms; text further down says he succeeded his father at 20 and died at 33 after conquering the world.
332 BC: the siege and fall of Tyre by Alexander; the chart says 8,000 were slain and 30,000 sold into slavery.
The first Roman military road, 350 miles long: the 'Appian Way', built by Appius Claudius in 312 BC.

entries.t: Onias I and Simon the Just
entries.p: The high priests Onias I and Simon 'the Just'.
The goat again, its great horn broken and four horns grown up (labeled Egypt, Greece, Asia Minor and Babylon and Syria), with a little horn; the chart dates Daniel's vision of chapter 8 to 555 BC.

entries.t: The fourth beast with ten horns
entries.p: A label for Daniel's fourth beast with ten horns.
Ptolemy I Lagus, called Soter ('Savior'), reigning 38 years; a note says he captured Jerusalem in 320 BC.
Two sides of a coin of Alexander the Great.
The Chinese wall built by Chi-Hoang-Ti, 263 to 236 BC; the chart gives it as 1,500 miles long, about 20 feet high, with towers every 300 feet.
Euclid of Alexandria, flourished 300 BC.
Seleucus I Nicator, reigning 32 years.
Achim on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Berosus, the Babylonian historian, 300 to 280 BC.
Zeno, the Stoic philosopher.
The label of the Jewish stream: Palestine or Judaea.
Ptolemy II Philadelphus, 38 years, who the chart says founded the Alexandrian Library.
The first Punic War, 264 BC, 23 years.
A picture of the Alexandrian Library, founded in 284 BC by Ptolemy Philadelphus with 700,000 volumes; the chart says it was partly burned by Julius Caesar in 47 BC and by Omar in AD 640.
The label of Syria under the Seleucids, 247 years, 312 to 65 BC.
Chi-Hoang-Ti, first emperor of China, 27 years.
The lighthouse of Alexandria, the seventh wonder, built by Ptolemy Philadelphus in 280 BC, 550 feet high.
Eliud on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
The brass Colossus of Rhodes, the sixth wonder (302-290 BC), 105 feet high; the chart says an earthquake threw it down in 224 BC and its metal was later sold and carried off on 900 camels.
Archimedes of Syracuse (287-212 BC) with drawings of his water screw and his lever.
The label of Bithynia, which the chart says was ruled in turn by the Assyrians, Lydians, Persians and Macedonians, and conquered by Rome in 74 BC.
Manetho, the Egyptian historian in the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus.
The label of Cappadocia in Asia Minor.
The label of Pergamus (Pergamum); a note says Eumenes II collected a library of 200,000 volumes.
The Parthian Empire founded by Arsaces in 250 BC; the chart says the Parthians were originally a tribe of Scythians.
Cannae, 216 BC: the Romans defeated by Hannibal.
A note that Alexandria in Egypt, with walls six miles around, was built by Alexander in 332 BC, who was buried there; it became the home of the Ptolemies.
The label of Egypt under the 13 Ptolemies, 323 to 30 BC, 293 years.
The second Punic War, 218 BC, 17 years.
Antiochus III the Great, reigning 36 years.
The fifth dynasty of China, the Han.
Hannibal, 37 years.
The label of Pontus.
The Rosetta Stone, black basalt, 3 by 2.5 feet, from 195 BC, discovered in AD 1799.
The chart notes the Sanhedrin is first mentioned in 198 BC.
Onias III, high priest.
Eleazar on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
A round map of the known world for Eratosthenes, the Alexandrian geographer (born 276, died 196 BC), who first planned the measuring of the earth.
146 BC: Greece made a Roman province under the name of Achaia; Corinth destroyed.
Hipparchus of Nicaea, who laid the foundations of geography and astronomy; flourished between 160 and 125 BC.
Jason, high priest from 175 BC.
A stream from Syria into Judaea reads: Jerusalem taken by Antiochus, 40,000 Jews slain, 170 BC.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, reigning 11 years.
Judas (Maccabeus), leading from 165 to 160 BC.
Demetrius I, reigning 12 years.
Polybius, Greek historian, born 203 BC.
The third Punic War, 149 BC, and Carthage taken by Scipio, 146 BC.
Antiochus V Eupator.

entries.t: Apocryphal history; daily sacrifice ceased and resumed
entries.p: The daily sacrifice ceased in 168 BC and resumed in 165 BC; the chart ends the history of the Apocrypha at 135 BC.

A table of Roman government for 1,229 years: Rome founded by Romulus in 753 BC, the kingdom ended and the republic began in 509 BC, the triumvirates, Octavius made emperor as Augustus Caesar, and the empire's end ('Fall of Rome') in AD 476.
Simon, high priest and governor.

entries.t: Explanation of the plan of the chart
entries.p: The chart's own key: the black line is the stream of time, black pillars mark each hundred years, red lines mark ten years, and nations are parallel streams that end when conquered. It then walks through Cyrus, Philip and Alexander as examples.
A clepsydra or water clock, set up at Rome in 158 BC by Scipio Nasica; a note adds that Alfred measured time by wax tapers.
Matthan on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Antiochus VII Sidetes, reigning 9 years.
A globe of the earth, half in shadow, drawn beside the astronomers and geographers.
A list of Sallust's works: the Catiline conspiracy, the Jugurthine war (112-106 BC) and his five books of Roman history (78-66 BC).
Hyrcanus, son of Simon, king and high priest.
166 BC: the government of the Maccabees begins; 161 BC: a treaty with the Romans, the first treaty with the Jews on record.

entries.t: John Hyrcanus destroys the temple on Mount Gerizim
entries.p: In 130 BC John Hyrcanus destroys the temple on Mount Gerizim.
Posidonius, philosopher and writer of Rhodes.
Janneus, king.
Mithridates VI 'the Great', king of Pontus, 60 years; the chart says he had all the Romans in Asia Minor killed in one day.
Sylla (Sulla): quaestor 107 BC, consul 88 BC, dictator 82 BC.
A portrait of Cicero, orator and philosopher, born 106 BC, 63 years.
A note on the first triumvirate of Julius Caesar, Crassus and Pompey in 60 BC, Caesar's rise and death in 44 BC, and Octavius becoming sole ruler and first emperor in 27 BC.
Jacob, father of Joseph the husband of Mary, on the line of Jesus' ancestors.
Julius Caesar, Crassus (consul) and Pompey (consul) share the stream of Rome as the first triumvirate, from 60 B.C.
Three men in long robes and turbans show how Hebrews dressed in the time of Jesus.
Wise men with camels point to a star above the town of Bethlehem. The caption quotes Matthew 2:2: wise men came from the east to Jerusalem saying they had seen his star and had come to worship him.
A flag marks 53 B.C. at "Carrhae," the battle where the Parthians defeated Crassus.

A royal barge with a canopy and rowers sails past a temple, under the heading "4004 A.M., Christian era begins." The caption says that after Cleopatra and Mark Antony were defeated at Actium, she killed herself by the bite of an asp in 30 B.C., making Octavius master of the world.
A laurel-crowned portrait sits above the bar for the poet Virgil, who lived 51 years and died in 19 B.C.
"J. Caesar invades Briton 55 B.C.," the first invasion of Britain; a note says he landed there twice.
A flag marks 47 B.C.: at Zela Caesar defeated Pharnaces and wrote "Veni, vidi, vici" (I came, I saw, I conquered).
An uncaptioned portrait of a young Roman sits just above the bar for the poet Horace, who lived 57 years and died in 8 B.C.
The Roman historian Livy, who lived 77 years, from 59 B.C. to A.D. 17.
Joseph, husband of Mary, on the family line that leads to Jesus.
A red flag marks 42 B.C.: "Philippi," where Octavius and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius.

entries.t: Cleopatra and the battle of Actium
entries.p: Egypt's stream ends with Cleopatra, queen 21 years. The note says Cleopatra and Antony were defeated at Actium in 31 B.C. and Egypt became a Roman province in 30 B.C.
Senators gather around Caesar's body beside a statue under a colonnade: "Caesar slain, 44 B.C."
A flag marks 31 B.C.: "Actium," where Octavius defeated Antony on September 2 and Egypt was subdued.
"Herod, King 34" heads the stream of Judea, after the Hasmonean rulers Alexandra and Hyrcanus, the Sanhedrin and Antipater.
A portrait of Julius Caesar. The caption says he was slain by Brutus, Cassius and others in the senate house on March 15, 44 B.C., falling at Pompey's statue with 23 wounds.
"Augustus Caesar, 1st emperor. The golden age of Rome. Emp. 44 yrs." He died August 19, A.D. 14.

entries.t: Archelaus and the procurators of Judea
entries.p: After Archelaus, Judea was governed by Roman procurators from A.D. 6: Coponius, Ambivius, Rufus, Gratus and the rest.
John the Baptist's bar ends in 32 with the note "beheaded."
A portrait labeled "Aug. Caesar," the emperor in whose reign Jesus was born.
A flag marks A.D. 9: Varus defeated by Arminius, the Germans' victory over three Roman legions.

A text panel says the Christian era began on January 1 in the middle of the 4th year of the 194th Olympiad, the 753rd year after Rome was built. It adds that Christ is now held to have been born 4 to 6 B.C.
"Jesus, 33, A.D." and "the Christ": the line of the Bible's genealogy ends here with Jesus.
"Tiberius Caesar, cruel and tyrannical," the second emperor, from A.D. 14, reigned 22 1/2 years.
Philo, a Jewish author, on the line of writers of the time.
Pontius Pilate appears as the fifth procurator of Judea, from the year 25.

A note says that in A.D. 70 Titus came to Jerusalem with an army of 60,000, causing the most horrible suffering since the world began: 1,100,000 died, and men were crucified until wood for crosses ran out.
The bar for the apostle Peter, who lived 75 years, ends in 68.
Lucius Seneca, who lived 64 years, "tutor of Nero, put to death by Nero" in A.D. 65.
The bar for the apostle Paul, who lived 60 years, ends in 68.
"King Agrippa" ruled Judea between the procurators, shown from 37 to 44.

entries.t: Pompeii and Herculaneum buried by Vesuvius
entries.p: A smoking volcano: "Pompei and Herculaneum buried by Vesuvius, Aug. 24th, 79 A.D., and Pliny smothered."
Pliny the Elder, shown from 23 to 79.
Strabo, a famous Greek historian and geographer, born in Cappadocia; the chart says his great geographical work fills 17 books.
The Coliseum in Rome, seating 80,000 to 100,000. The caption says it was begun by Vespasian and finished by his son Titus about A.D. 79.
Claudius, the fourth emperor, from 41 to 54.

entries.t: Anno Domini: the crucifixion of Jesus
entries.p: A large picture of Jesus on the cross marks the start of the Christian era (Anno Domini). The sign above him reads "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" in English and Latin (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, INRI).
The bar for the apostle John, "the author of Revelation," runs to the year 99.
An uncaptioned picture of a charioteer driving four galloping horses.
Barnabas's bar ends with a note that he was stoned to death about A.D. 60, according to tradition.
The procurators Felix and Porcius Festus, before whom Paul was tried, shown from 52 to 70.
"Nero, profligate tyrant (suicide)," the fifth emperor, reigned 14 years from 54.
"Parthian Empire (sixth oriental monarchy)": the stream of Parthia, Rome's great rival in the east.
The Jewish historian Josephus, shown living from 37 to 95.
Plutarch the biographer; a note says his "Parallel Lives" holds the lives of 46 famous Greeks and Romans set in pairs.

entries.t: First persecution, under Nero; martyrdom of Paul
entries.p: A red cross marks the first persecution, by Nero, 64 to 68, with the label "martyrdom of Paul."

entries.t: First council of the apostles at Jerusalem
entries.p: A red ring marks the first council of the apostles at Jerusalem in A.D. 50, citing Acts 15.
Vespasian, the ninth emperor, reigned 10 years from 69.

entries.t: Who invented the era of A.D.
entries.p: A text panel says the era of A.D. was invented by Dionysius Exiguus about 532 (or 527). It says the bishops' council of Chelsea ordered its use in 816, and that Charles III of Germany first added "in the year of our Lord" to his reign in 879.
St. Clement (Greek), called a co-laborer of Paul, whose bar ends in 101.
Ignatius was made bishop of Antioch in 69, the chart says, and the cross after his bar marks his death in 107.
A portrait of the emperor Nero.
"Flavius Domitian, last of the 12 Caesars," brother of Titus, murdered; he reigned 15 years.
Tacitus, Roman consul and historian, whose bar ends in 120; the panel below lists his surviving works.

entries.t: Jerusalem taken and destroyed by Titus
entries.p: Roman soldiers storm the walls of a burning city: "Jerusalem taken and destroyed by Titus, Sep. 8, 70 A.D."
A Roman coin reading "IVDEA CAPTA" (Judea captured), showing a Roman soldier and a mourning woman under a palm tree.

entries.t: Second persecution, under Domitian; John banished to Patmos
entries.p: A red cross marks the second persecution, under Domitian, 95 to 96, with the note "banishment of John to Patmos."
A red cross marks the third persecution, under Trajan, 106 to 107.
"Trajan, great sovereign; the empire in its greatest extent," reigned 19 years from 98.
"Ptolemy Claudius," a celebrated Roman astronomer and geographer born in Egypt.
A Roman soldier carries a standard topped by an eagle and marked S.P.Q.R.: "Senatus Populusque Romanus," the Roman senate and people.
"Adrian" (Hadrian), the 14th emperor, who rebuilt Jerusalem, put a temple of Jupiter on the site of Solomon's temple, and visited Britain; he reigned 21 years.
An open book: "New Testament, 27 books in 1 vol., by 8 authors, 52 A.D. to 96 A.D.," with a line from Byron calling it the "awful volume" of mysteries.
"Justin the Martyr," who lived 66 years and died in 166, born at Sychar in Samaria.
Polycarp, "disciple of John," whose bar ends with a cross in 167.
"Trajan's Column, built A.D. 114, 140 ft. high."
A drawing of the Roman Forum as it may have looked, with temples and colonnades.
A wooden plow on wheels: "Roman plow (described by Pliny)."
"Titus Antoninus Pius, eminent for his virtues, prosperous and equitable reign," the 15th emperor, reigned 23 years.
A diagram of the universe with the earth at the center inside rings of planets and stars: "Ptolemaic system: that the earth was the common center and the sun, moon and stars revolved around it."
Irenaeus, disciple of Polycarp and bishop of Lyons in France from 177, who wrote five books against heresies.
A red cross marks the fourth persecution, under Aurelius, 166 to 177.
The triumphal arch built in Rome for Titus, who took Jerusalem.
"Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, a virtuous Stoic philosopher," the 16th emperor, reigned 19 years.
"Claudius Galenus (Galen), 88," the celebrated Greek physician, who the note says wrote 500 books on medicine.
"Titus Flavius Clement" (Greek), whose bar ends in 220.
The great round tomb of the emperor Hadrian in Rome: "Adrian's tomb."
Commodus, son of Marcus Aurelius, "profligate and cruel," whose reign began the decline; murdered.
Tertullian, who lived 60 years (160 to 220), a lawyer and then priest of Carthage, who wrote 30 treatises.
Both sides of a Jewish shekel, labeled "Shekel or 'piece of silver' (53 cts.)."
"Septimus Severus, a brave man," who visited Britain in 208, built a wall and died at York.
"Roman Empire, from Romulus 753 B.C. to Augustus Romulus 476 A.D. (1229 yrs.); from Aug. Caesar 30 B.C. to Aug. Romulus 476 A.D. (506 yrs.)."
A red cross marks the fifth persecution, under Severus, 200 to 211.
Origen, who lived 67 years (186 to 253), born at Alexandria, who preached at Caesarea and died at Tyre.
A Roman lady in a long red gown holding a parasol: "Roman belle."
Cyprian, born at Carthage, elected bishop there in 248 and martyred September 14, 258.
A red cross marks the sixth persecution, under Maximinus, 235 to 237.

entries.t: Commodus entering the lists as a gladiator
entries.p: The emperor Commodus fights as a gladiator in an arena before crowds. The caption says such games were abolished by Honorius in 404.

entries.t: Map of the world by Ptolemy
entries.p: A small map of Europe, Asia and Africa as Ptolemy drew it. The caption calls him the most celebrated writer on astronomy, geography and chronology of ancient times, whose books were used for 1400 years.
A red cross marks the seventh persecution, under Decius, 250 to 253.
Soldiers strike down the emperor Aurelian: "Aurelian assassinated."
A red cross marks the eighth persecution, under Valerian, 257 to 260.
A list of the Christian apologists: Quadratus, Aristides, Justin Martyr, Melito of Sardis, Claudius Apollinaris, Athenagoras, Miltiades, Theophilus of Antioch, Tatian and Hermias.
Porphyry, pupil of Origen and Plotinus, born at Tyre, who wrote 15 books against Christianity at Rome; the note says Theodosius destroyed them.
A flag marks 260: Valerian defeated and captured by Sapor, king of Persia.
A red cross marks the ninth persecution, under Aurelian, in 275.
A bare, chained man stands by a column: "Valerian, flayed alive by Sapor, 260."
Diocletian, who took power in 284 (the start of the "Diocletian era"), took Maximian as co-ruler in 286 and began the "last and worst persecution"; the two later gave up the throne.
Eusebius (Greek), who lived 70 years from 270, born at Caesarea, author of over 45 books; the note says he baptized Constantine the Great.
Arius, who opposed the consubstantiality (same essence) of the Son with the Father; his bar ends in 336.
A flag marks 323: at Adrianople Constantine defeats Licinius.
A portrait medallion beside the note on St. George, patron saint of England, a supposed prince of Cappadocia beheaded by Diocletian in 290.
A red cross marks the tenth persecution, under Diocletian, 303 to 313, begun at Nicomedia: churches torn down and the rack, fire and sword used.
"Constantine the Great, first Christian emperor," who moved the capital to Constantinople in 330 A.D. and died May 22, 337.
A portrait: "Heliogabalus, wanton, extravagant, depraved and horribly cruel."
A flag marks 312: Constantine defeats Maxentius.
A cross marked "In hoc signo vinces" (in this sign conquer) and a kneeling man: "Constantine's conversion, by a vision of a luminous cross in the sky, 313."
A Roman senator in a toga holding a scroll, beside his wife spinning thread with a distaff: "Senator's wife spinning."
"Scriptures translated by Jerome about 405 into Latin, called the 'Latin Vulgate,' then translated into English at Douay in 1609; the only English version sanctioned by the Roman Catholic church."
Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, who lived 77 years (296 to 373) and held the office 46 years.

Bishops gather before an altar under a halo marked "Jesus Hominum Salvator" (Jesus, Savior of men). "1st Ecumenical Council at Nice, Bithynia, called by Constantine; present 318 bishops; the 'Nicene Creed' formed A.D. 325."
A man sits locked in the stocks while another taunts him. The caption says stocks were used in the time of Job (Job 13:27) and the last ones in London were removed August 4, 1826.
A Roman warship with a square sail, shields along its side and a bird-headed prow: "Roman galley."
"St. Basil the Great" (Greek), 326 to 379.
"Gregory Nazianzen" (Greek), 328 to 389.
A hooded scholar writes at a desk: "Hieronymus or Jerome, 90," who wrote on almost every subject; his bar ends in 420.
St. Ambrose (Latin), who lived 57 years, to 397.
A Roman woman's braided hair with a jeweled band, "head dress," with a laced Roman boot below it.
A red ring: "2nd Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, May to July 381 A.D., 150 bishops attend."
A portrait of the emperor Theodosius.
Chrysostom, born at Antioch, patriarch of Constantinople, called "the golden-mouthed" orator; his bar ends in 407.
Augustine, who lived 76 years, bishop of Hippo, the most famous of the Latin fathers; his bar ends in 430.
"Ephraim Syrus," a Greek father, who died about 378.
A red ring: "3rd Ecumenical Council at Ephesus, 431 A.D."
St. Cyril of Alexandria (Greek), author of works against the Nestorians; his bar ends in 444.
Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople 429, condemned and deposed at the third council at Ephesus because he did not believe Mary was the mother of Jesus as God.
A red stream labeled "Alaric and Goths in Rome 410" pours toward Rome; the note says Rome was captured by Alaric in 410 and given up to six days of plunder.
Theodosius II, cousin of Valentinian, who gave the Theodosian code of laws; in his reign Attila, the "scourge of God," ravaged the land between the Euxine and the Adriatic.
"Roman or Western Empire, capitals Milan and Ravenna," the western half after the empire was divided.
Round stone huts with cone-shaped thatched roofs: "Celtic houses of France, 500 B.C. to 600 A.D."
A red ring: "4th Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon, 451," Chalcedon being in Asia Minor opposite Byzantium.
Armed warriors with round shields land from a ship while Britons resist: "Saxons invade England 449."
A bishop with raised hand preaches to kneeling men beside a cross: "St. Patrick in Ireland about 432 A.D."

A portrait of Attila in a pointed helmet: "Attila dies 453, 'the scourge of God.'" The note says the Huns under Attila ravaged Europe and were defeated at Chalons in 451, the last great battle fought by the Romans.
A flag marks 451: "Chalons-sur-Marne," where Attila and his hordes were defeated by Aetius.
"Greek or Eastern Empire, Constantinople the capital," the eastern half that went on after the West fell.

"The Romans leave Britain about 426 A.D. when the Picts and Scots invade from the north. The Saxons being invited over to assist in expelling them gradually take possession of the country, and the Saxon Heptarchy is formed and exists till Egbert forms the Kingdom of England in 827."

entries.t: Odoacer and the end of the Western Empire
entries.p: "Odoacer, king, 17": the Western Roman Empire's stream ends at 476 when Odoacer takes Italy.
Clovis, who founded the Frank monarchy with Paris as its capital and married Clotilda, a Catholic princess; a note says he was baptized with 3000 of his soldiers on Christmas Day, 496.
An uncaptioned drawing of a draped elephant carrying two riders in turbans.
"Theodoric the Great" of the Ostrogothic monarchy of Italy, who gave one third of the lands to his 500,000 troops.

Three bare-chested warriors with shields, spear and axe: "Ancient savage Britons." The note above says the Celts were Britain's first inhabitants, clothed in skins, and that their religion was Druidism.
"Fathers" from the Latin and Greek fathers we have extracts of many earlier writers whose works are now lost; they are a link to us in the historic chain.
"Justinian, 38," who married Theodora; the "Justinian Code" was drawn up by 10 lawyers under Tribonian in 534.

entries.t: Chariot of the "lazy kings" of France
entries.p: Oxen draw a covered wagon with a king inside, guarded by a horseman: "Chariot of the 'lazy kings' of France, 6th and 7th centuries."

Cosmas, an Egyptian monk of the 6th century, who wrote a "Topography of the World" to refute the "impious doctrine of the earth's sphericity"; he argued the earth was a vast plain surrounded by a wall.
A red ring: "5th Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, 553."
An old blind man with a child on his shoulders: "Belisarius, begging his daily bread," Justinian's great general.
A scroll marked "Koran 610."
Ethelbert, "Rex Anglorum" (king of the English), a Christian king of Kent who married Bertha, daughter of Caribert.
A crucifix marks St. Augustine, who arrived in England in 596 with 40 monks, sent by Gregory the Great.
A rider on a camel: "The 'Hegira' 622, Mecca to Medina," Thursday night, July 15, 622; the era of the Hegira begins July 16, 622.
A turbaned man with raised hand: "Mahomet, Hegira 622," born 569 or 570.
A ring of standing stones: "Stonehenge at Amesbury, Eng., Druid temple (restored), an ancient temple of the Britons in which the Druids officiated."
A note says the "vulgar Christian era" was invented about 532 by Dionysius Exiguus, a monk; chronologers agree it is 4 years too late for the birth of Christ.
Heraclius, Eastern emperor for 31 years from 610.
"Of Vandal origin, from the north: Lombard Kingdom of Italy."
A domed building "from a photograph": "Mosque built by Omar 637 on the spot of Solomon's Temple."

A note says Jerusalem was taken by Titus in 70 A.D. and razed, with more than 1,000,000 Jews killed; taken by the Saracens in 637, by the Crusaders in 1099, by Saladin in 1187 and by the Turks in 1516.
Omar I, caliph for 10 years; the streams of Egypt, Palestine, Syria and Arabia, provinces lost by the Eastern Empire, flow into his Saracen empire.
A red ring: "6th Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, Nov. 7, 680 to Feb. 28, 681, vs. the Monothelites."
A tall Gothic college building: "Cambridge University, founded 630?"
Notes on when arithmetic came from Egypt into Greece, when paper was invented in China, and how the bank (from "banco," a bench in the market) began in Italy.
Text panels on Saxony, a kingdom in north Germany whose fierce people conquered Britain, and on Bavaria, with a list of its rulers.
Bede, "the Venerable," born in Northumbria, England, a great writer and scholar, 672 to 735.
Drawings of four old coins captioned "Ancient coins, one 'source' of history."
